# Service Repositioning — Regional Market
## Internal codename: **"Fewer Reasons to Ask"**

**Version 1. Draft for correction, not for approval.** Complete in structure; every number is a placeholder with a named owner.

**Circulated for correction to:** Customer Care (regional and Group), Operations/Fulfilment, Logistics & Last Mile, Returns, Payments, Product/App, Insight, Data, Local Commercial lead, Finance business partner, Legal/Consumer Regulatory, Data Protection, People, Corporate Affairs.

**Approval route:** local pod decides inside the guardrails in §12 → Steering group at gates only → Executive Committee for the guarantee clause (§3.2) and the data-residency choice (§6.3) only. Nothing else in this document requires a committee, and the programme will move faster if that is respected.

**Convention on numbers.** Every figure is a percentage of *regional contact volume*, a percentage of the *regional service cost base*, or basis points of *regional gross order value (GOV)*. No absolute currency figures appear anywhere. The functions that own the P&L substitute real values without re-deriving the logic. Assumption register with named owners: Annex A.

**On the codename.** "Fewer Reasons to Ask" is an internal working title. It is not a customer promise, not a tagline, and must not appear in any external material. Customer-facing language is written and tested at Gate 2 (§3.2), and only against what is by then already true.

---

## Decision sheet — one page

**Recommendation.** Do not buy a better help desk. Remove the reasons the customer had to open it, and change who is allowed to say yes.

The regional feedback is being read internally as *"our support is not good enough."* That reading leads predictably to a channel purchase, a chatbot, a CSAT target and a communications moment. It is worth entertaining a less flattering reading: that most contacts in this market are **failure demand** — the customer is not seeking help, they are chasing something we already broke upstream — and that the contacts that *are* genuine are being handled by people who lack the authority, the language register and the local knowledge to close them. If that is what the record says, then a better help desk makes the wrong thing more efficient.

So the proposal is: **fix the causes, collapse the escalation tiers, answer in the customer's own idiom and channel, publish the record of what we changed — and say nothing externally until it has been true for eight consecutive weeks.**

**Four gates. No spend beyond gate cost is released until the prior gate passes.**

| Gate | What it tests | Duration | Cost | Decision sought now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Gate 0 — Contact Truth Audit** (§2) | What our own record already says: reason-for-contact taxonomy, repeat-contact chains, unresolved tails, register/translation quality, promises previously made and not kept | Weeks 1–5 | ~0.5–1.0% of regional service cost base | Fund it; mandate unedited access to transcripts, recordings, returns and last-mile data |
| **Gate 1 — Diagnostic** (§1.2) | Whether the gap is upstream defect, channel absence, authority, register/cultural fit, or expectation set by a local competitor | Weeks 1–8 | ~1.0–2.0% of service cost base | Fund it, and accept in advance that the answer may move most of the money out of Customer Care and into Logistics, Payments and Returns |
| **Gate 2 — Charter & guarantee sign-off** (§3.2) | What we can honestly promise, at what auto-compensation cost | Month 3 | Inside Gate 1 budget | Agree the promise is written at month 3 against evidence, not at month 0 against ambition |
| **Gate 3 — Pilot readout** (§9.2) | Whether the effect is real in a held-out design, not a seasonal artefact | Months 4–6 | ~2–3% of service cost base | Agree the scale/stop thresholds **now** (§10.2), while no one is invested in the answer |

**Money, in percentage terms (planning case — to be replaced at Gate 1).**

| | Year 1 | Year 2 | Steady state |
|---|---|---|---|
| Programme cost (audit, upstream fixes, channel build, authority/goodwill pool, local hiring & training, tooling, community layer) | 7–10% of regional service cost base | 5–7% | 3–4% |
| Funded by failure-demand elimination (contacts removed, not deflected) | 2–3% | 6–9% | 9–13% |
| Funded by reallocation inside existing Care and regional marketing budgets | 3–4% | 3–4% | 3–4% |
| **Net incremental cash ask** | **1–4% of regional service cost base** | **nil to 1%** | **nil (net saving)** |
| Expressed against revenue, for comparability | ~1–4 bps of regional GOV | ~0–1 bps | negative (saving) |
| Plus: auto-compensation and goodwill exposure (§3.2, §4C) | 3–8 bps of regional GOV | 2–6 bps | 2–5 bps |

**What is being asked for today:** funding for Gates 0 and 1 (together ~1.5–3.0% of the regional service cost base), the four decision rights in §12.1, and agreement in principle to the sequencing rule: **proof first, promise second, announcement last — if at all.**

**What is being asked for the authority to refuse:**
1. A market-wide service announcement, brand campaign or "we've listened" moment before Gate 3.
2. An average-CSAT target as the programme's headline goal (§7.2 explains why this metric will actively damage the work).
3. A chatbot mandate expressed as a deflection or containment percentage.
4. Relocation of this market's contact handling to a lower-cost centre during the pilot window.

---

## 1. Diagnosis

### 1.1 The distinction the whole plan rests on

Two kinds of contact arrive at the same queue and are counted identically:

- **Value demand** — the customer wants something from us that we should want to give: advice, sizing, a suitability question, a change of mind, a genuine choice. This demand is *revenue-adjacent* and should be answered generously, slowly if needed, by a human.
- **Failure demand** — the customer is contacting us because we already failed: the parcel is late or lost, the address logic broke, the refund did not arrive, the promotion did not apply, the app rejected a local payment method, the return window assumed a courier network that does not operate here. This demand is *pure cost plus reputational damage*, and it is almost never a Customer Care defect in origin.

In most mass e-commerce operations, failure demand runs somewhere between 55% and 75% of total contact volume. If this market sits at the upper end, then the honest description of the situation is not "support underperforms" but "support absorbs the operational cost of our own defects, and the customer experiences the absorption as the defect."

**Every intervention in §4 is sorted by that distinction.** Section A removes failure demand. Sections B–E make value demand worth having.

### 1.2 Four rival explanations, weighted before commitment

| Rival diagnosis | Test at Gate 1 | Implication if it dominates |
|---|---|---|
| **Upstream defect, not service** | Reason-for-contact taxonomy; % of contacts traceable to a fulfilment, payment, returns or content root cause; repeat-contact chains per order | The plan is a Logistics/Payments/Returns plan with a small Care component. Budget moves. Nobody loses standing for finding this |
| **Channel absence** | Where support conversations in this market actually happen — dominant messaging apps, voice notes, social DMs, marketplace inboxes, community forums — versus where we are present | Channel presence becomes the plan (§4B). Content and tone follow later, cheaply |
| **Authority, not effort** | Distribution of resolution outcomes by handler tier; % of contacts requiring ≥2 touches; time-to-*truth* (not time-to-first-reply); % of first replies that resolve nothing | Collapse the tiers and fund frontline discretion (§4C). This is the cheapest high-yield intervention available |
| **Register and cultural fit** | Blind review of transcripts by local-language reviewers: formality level, dialect, honorifics, machine-translation artefacts, culturally wrong apology form, script rigidity | Hire and train locally; rewrite the response library from scratch in-market rather than translating it (§4B, §5) |
| **Expectation, set elsewhere** | Benchmarked local norms: what the dominant regional player or marketplace has taught customers to expect on response time, returns friction, cash/COD handling, human availability | We are being measured against a local standard, not a global one. Set the promise against the local standard (§3.2) |

Realistically the answer is a weighting across all five. **Pre-agreed Gate 1 rule:** if upstream defect plus channel absence together explain more than half of the modelled satisfaction gap, that is stated in writing, the money is redirected, and the redirection is recorded as a *success* of the diagnostic rather than a retreat.

### 1.3 The regional customer, segmented — and the honest limit of service investment

Service investment does not move everyone equally. Sizing this before, not after, prevents the familiar outcome where a well-built programme is judged against a prize it was never able to win.

| Segment | Hypothesised share of regional buyers | What actually moves them | What this programme gives them |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Recoverable defectors** — had one bad experience, still buying occasionally or lapsed within 12 months | 15–25% | A resolution that arrives without them chasing; visible evidence the cause was fixed | The core target. Recovery mechanics (§4C), proactive contact (§4A), the published record (§4D) |
| **Habitual, low-contact** | 40–50% | Nothing going wrong; frictionless repurchase | Failure-demand elimination. They will never notice the programme, and that is the point |
| **High-involvement / advice-seeking** — pre-purchase questions, high basket, high return rate | 10–15% | Expertise, memory of prior conversations, a named human | Value-demand investment (§4B, §4E). Best margin response per unit of effort |
| **Price-first, platform-promiscuous** | 20–30% | Absolute price and delivery speed | Very little. Service investment will not hold them, and the programme should not be charged with trying |

**Consequence.** Roughly a quarter to two-fifths of the base is genuinely addressable by service quality; for the largest group the correct service experience is *no service experience*. If Gate 1 finds recoverable defectors below 10% of the regional base, the human-investment portion of the programme is halved and reweighted into upstream defect removal.

### 1.4 What we are actually competing with

Not global service benchmarks. In a regional market the relevant comparators are usually: the dominant local marketplace's handling norms; a local player with physical presence and therefore trivially easy returns; and, quietly, the informal channel — the WhatsApp/messaging-app seller who answers personally in eleven minutes at nine in the evening.

That last comparator is the instructive one. It has no CRM, no tiering and no scripts, and it beats us on the only three things customers describe as service: *a human, quickly, who can actually decide.* Everything in §4C is an attempt to reproduce those three properties at scale without pretending to be small.

---

## 2. Gate 0 — the Contact Truth Audit

**The risk.** We are about to design a service promise for a market whose actual failure pattern we have described in aggregate satisfaction scores. Aggregate scores are the least informative artefact we hold. Worse, we may have made service promises here before — response-time claims, returns language, a "we've listened" communication — that were not kept. Publishing a new promise on top of a broken one is not a fresh start; it is the second offence, and customers keep receipts.

**Five weeks, evidence-first, worst case surfaced on purpose.**

| Workstream | Owner | Deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| Reason-for-contact taxonomy, coded to root cause and to the owning function | Insight / Data | Contact volume split value vs failure demand; top ten root causes ranked by volume × repeat rate × downstream churn |
| Repeat-contact archaeology | Care Ops | Distribution of touches-per-issue; the long tail of issues taking ≥4 touches; what those cases have in common |
| The unresolved tail | Care Ops / Data | Cases closed without resolution or closed by customer abandonment; what happened to those customers' next 90 days of spend |
| Silent defectors | Data / Insight | Customers who had a failure event and *never contacted us* — volume, and their subsequent purchase behaviour. This cohort is usually larger than the complaining cohort and is invisible in CSAT |
| Register and translation audit | Local team, blind-reviewed | Sample of transcripts scored by in-market reviewers for formality, dialect, machine-translation artefacts, apology form, script rigidity |
| Promise history | Corporate Affairs / Legal / Marketing | Every service commitment made in this market, with evidence of whether it was met. So that we do not contradict ourselves |
| Frontline testimony | People / Care | Unattributed, unedited: what the frontline already knows about why customers contact us and what they are prevented from doing about it |

**Pre-agreed decision rules, set now so they are not negotiated later under pressure:**

| Audit finding | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Failure demand >60% of volume, concentrated in ≤5 root causes | Programme is re-chartered as an upstream defect programme with a service component. Budget authority shifts accordingly |
| Prior unmet public service promise exists | The first external act is a specific, unprompted acknowledgement of that gap with evidence of the fix — before any new promise is made |
| Register/translation quality materially poor | No new channel opens until the response library is rewritten in-market. Adding channels to a bad voice multiplies the bad voice |
| Silent-defector cohort large and value-dense | Proactive detection (§4A.4) is promoted above channel expansion in the sequence |
| The record is too thin to answer these questions | That is itself the finding. Instrumentation becomes the first deliverable, and no promise is published for at least one further quarter |

**One cultural note, said once.** This audit will surface decisions that were rational when made and are indefensible now, and it will surface individual handling that looks poor out of context. Amnesty on history; no amnesty on concealment. A root cause known internally and discovered externally is the failure mode that ends programmes and damages the people inside them.

---

## 3. The proposition

### 3.1 The idea

> **Answered here, by someone who can decide, before you have to ask twice.**

Three claims, each independently verifiable, each costed in §4. *Here* is local — language, register, hours, knowledge of the actual courier network. *Someone who can decide* is authority, not empathy training.

## 1. Diagnosis

The brief says the brand is "seen as outdated." That diagnosis produced the last two campaigns, and it should be tested rather than inherited.

Under-35s do not reject old things. They pay premiums for them — vinyl, film cameras, workwear, cast iron, archive product, an inherited watch. What they reject is pretending. The previous campaigns were not punished for being old-fashioned; they were punished for borrowing youth codes the brand had not earned. The loyal base felt betrayed for exactly the same reason: they watched the brand disown itself in public and correctly read that as an admission that being itself was insufficient. Both audiences were reacting to the same defect.

So the useful reframe for the internal disagreement is not *"how much change can the brand absorb?"* but *"how much of what we already own have we failed to make interesting?"* That question asks no one to surrender the heritage, and it licenses substantial change everywhere except identity. It has given both internal camps somewhere to stand in the conversations held so far, and §13.3 sets out how the residual disagreement is settled by evidence rather than by seniority.

### 1.1 Before spending anything: is this a brand problem?

Three alternative explanations must be weighted before commitment. Sales and Category have already pointed at two of them.

| Alternative diagnosis | Test in the data | Implication if it dominates |
|---|---|---|
| **Presence, not meaning** | Under-35 category spend share by channel vs our distribution weight: marketplace, quick-commerce, convenience, social commerce, DTC/subscription | Channel and listing plan becomes the plan; brand work becomes a light supporting layer at a fraction of cost and time (§7) |
| **Life-stage, not cohort** | Age-standardised penetration: does today's 30-year-old buy at roughly the rate the 30-year-old of a decade ago did? | The prize is smaller than assumed. Scale the programme down, and calm the internal alarm rather than feeding it |
| **Format and occasion fit** | Pack size, price-per-use, prep or use time against single/dual-occupancy urban households | Pack architecture and adjacent formats, not repositioning (§5.3) |

In most real cases the answer is a weighting across all four causes. The weighting sets the budget. **Gate 1 rule, agreed in advance:** if availability and format fit together explain more than half of the modelled under-35 gap, we say so in writing, redirect the money, and no one loses standing for it. The diagnostic is the reason we looked.

### 1.2 The under-35 prize, segmented — and the honest limit of this positioning

A standards argument does not recruit everybody. It historically recruits information-seeking, higher-involvement buyers. If most of our under-35 gap sits with price-first shoppers, this positioning comforts the base and recruits a thin slice. That must be sized before, not after.

Working hypothesis, for Insight to size and correct at Gate 1:

| Under-35 segment | Hypothesised share of under-35 category buyers | What actually moves them | What this programme gives them |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Provenance-led** — reads labels, researches, screenshots reformulation threads, willing to pay per-use premiums | 20–25% | Verifiable proof, published record, refusal to cut corners | The whole positioning. This is the recruitment target |
| **Convenience-first urban** — low deliberation, high immediacy, small households | 35–40% | Availability at the moment of need, right pack size, frictionless repurchase | Channel presence and adjacent formats (§5.3, §7.1). Meaning is a light coating, not the mechanism |
| **Price-first, private-label fluent** | 35–40% | Absolute price and perceived parity | The everyday entry pack (§5.2) and nothing more. We do not chase this segment with meaning money, and we should stop pretending campaigns will convert it |

**Consequence.** The positioning is the recruitment engine for roughly a quarter of the under-35 pool and the retention engine for the whole existing base. Channel and format work carry the larger volume. Both are funded here, and the programme should be judged on the combination — not on the campaign. If Gate 1 finds the provenance-led segment is materially smaller than 15% of under-35 category buyers, the meaning investment is halved and reweighted to availability.

### 1.3 The real competitor is private label, not premium heritage

For a mass-distributed heritage brand, the mechanism of decline is own-label and dupe substitution, not a niche premium challenger. This must sit at the centre of the competitive case.

- **Private label's structural weakness is exactly our claim.** Own-label economics require periodic re-tendering of specification: suppliers rotate, grades move with commodity cycles, formulations are re-optimised silently. Continuity is not something the model can promise. We can promise it, publish it and have it verified (§12.2). That is a genuine asymmetry, and it is the only durable answer to "it's the same thing for 30% less."
- **Price-gap discipline replaces promotional depth.** The defensible instrument is a *permanent* everyday entry pack that holds the realised price gap to own label inside an agreed band (§5.2), not periodic deep discounting that teaches the shopper our real price is the promoted one.
- **Premium heritage brands are a source of craft reference, not a competitive set.** Their economics are not ours; benchmarking against them will mislead the plan. Our position is heritage *and* ubiquity — "the everyday thing that never got worse" — which no premium niche brand and no own-label programme currently occupies.

## 2. Gate 0 — the Truth Audit (this comes before positioning is signed)

**The risk.** "The brand that was never cheapened" is currently an assertion, not a verified fact. Almost no seventy-year-old mass brand has left pack weight, sourcing, grade and formulation untouched across seven decades. If we publish an absolute claim and a consumer produces a 1998 pack photograph, we generate precisely the authenticity backlash this programme exists to prevent — and this time we will have invited it in writing, under our own signature. This is the single largest risk in the document.

**Therefore, nothing external is committed until the record is known.**

**Scope of the audit — six weeks, evidence-based, worst case surfaced deliberately.**

| Workstream | Owner | Deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| Formulation and specification history of the hero SKU, decade by decade | R&D | Change log with dates, reasons, and whether each change was a downgrade, a neutral substitution or an improvement |
| Pack weight, fill and unit-count history | Category / Packaging | Grammage timeline against price timeline — the shrinkflation exposure, stated plainly |
| Sourcing, grade and origin history; factory locations and moves | Procurement / Operations | Continuity map; every discontinuity documented |
| Quality performance history | Quality | Complaint and reject-rate trend; any period of genuine deterioration |
| Public claim history | Corporate Affairs / Legal | Every historical quality claim made, so that we do not contradict our own advertising |
| Consumer memory | Customer Care / Insight | Complaint archive mined for "it's not what it used to be" — dated, thematised. This is the map of where we are vulnerable |

**The pre-agreed decision rule — set now, so it is not negotiated under pressure later.**

| Audit outcome | Positioning consequence |
|---|---|
| **Clean:** no material downgrade to the hero SKU's specification, grade or per-use quality | Publish the absolute claim, with the record attached. Strongest case |
| **Narrow blemish:** isolated changes, defensible or neutral, one or two exposures | Claim narrows to the specific verifiable attributes ("same formula, same grade, same origin since 19XX"), and we publish the exceptions ourselves, first, before anyone finds them |
| **Material downgrade, since corrected** | Position becomes **"the standard we restored — here is the whole record."** Weaker, but survivable and arguably more credible. Requires the restoration to be real and demonstrable |
| **Material downgrade, uncorrected** | The positioning cannot be published. Choose: fund the restoration and then claim it, or abandon this route entirely. There is no version where we assert it and hope |

**Cultural point, said once and plainly:** the audit will be uncomfortable for colleagues who authorised past changes, most of which were rational at the time. It is not a search for fault, and it should not be run as one. It is framed as protecting the people who will have to stand behind the claim. Amnesty on history, no amnesty on concealment — a change discovered externally that was known internally is the failure mode that ends the programme and damages the people in it. That is worth saying openly at the start.

## 1. Fatal defect: the document does not answer the request

The brief asked for **innovative approaches and improvements to customer service** in a regional market. What has been delivered is a governance apparatus and a diagnostic frame. The output terminates mid-sentence in §3.1. Every section containing actual interventions is referenced but absent:

- §4A (failure-demand removal), §4B (channel/register), §4C (authority/recovery), §4D (published record), §4E (value demand) — all cited repeatedly, none written
- §5 (response library), §6.3 (data residency), §7.2 (metrics), §9.2 (pilot design), §10.2 (scale/stop thresholds), §12.1 (decision rights), Annex A (assumption register)

The header claims "Complete in structure." It is not. As it stands, a reader learns *how the programme will be governed* and *why the problem may be misdiagnosed*, but not one concrete thing the company would actually do differently for a customer. That alone requires major revision.

## 2. Arithmetic errors in the money table

The funding table does not reconcile.

- **Year 1:** cost 7–10%, funding 2–3% + 3–4% = 5–7%. True net range is **0–5%**, not the stated "1–4%."
- **Year 2:** cost 5–7%, funding 6–9% + 3–4% = **9–13%**. That is a net *surplus of 2–8%*, not "nil to 1%." The row is wrong by construction.
- **Steady state:** cost 3–4% against funding 12–17% → an 8–14% net saving, described only as "nil (net saving)." The document understates its own business case by an order of magnitude, which is worse than overstating it — it invites Finance to conclude the author has not read the table.
- **Gate costs vs programme cost:** Gates 0–3 total 3.5–6.0% of the service cost base. Are these inside the 7–10% Year-1 line or additive? Unstated. A funding ask cannot be ambiguous on this point.
- **Unit bridge is broken.** "1–4% of regional service cost base ≈ 1–4 bps of GOV" implies the service cost base equals exactly 1% of GOV. That hidden assumption is doing enormous work. If the cost base is 2–3% of GOV (common in mass e-commerce), the bps figures are wrong by 2–3×. Declare the ratio as a named assumption or delete the row.
- **Internal contradiction on savings logic.** §1.1 asserts failure demand is 55–75% of volume. Steady-state savings of only 9–13% of the cost base implies eliminating roughly a sixth of failure demand — far below what the intervention set implies. Either the savings are understated or "contacts removed" has been silently converted into cost at a poor rate. Resolve explicitly, because this is the number the whole self-funding claim rests on.

## 3. Segment shares are impossible

15–25 + 40–50 + 10–15 + 20–30 = **85–120%**. The upper bound exceeds the population. (This error is inherited from the prior document, where 20–25 + 35–40 + 35–40 = 90–105%.) If segments are mutually exclusive, constrain the ranges to sum to 100%; if they overlap, say so and stop presenting them as a partition.

## 4. Template transfer rather than problem-specific thinking

The document is a structural clone of "Older Than the Noise": same decision sheet, same "Truth Audit" gate, same "amnesty on history, no amnesty on concealment," same "the honest limit of…" section, same "price-first" segment that the programme declines to chase, same "what we are asking for the authority to refuse." Some of that scaffolding travels well. Some does not, and it has been carried across unexamined:

- A **70-year archival audit** makes sense for a heritage claim. A five-week contact audit is a different animal and should not be dressed in the same "seventy years of evidence" costume.
- The **"no launch moment"** rule was right for a brand that had twice been punished for premature campaigns. Here it is asserted, not argued from this market's history — and it directly conflicts with the Gate 0 rule that the *first external act* must be an unprompted acknowledgement of a prior broken promise. Which comes first: silence for eight weeks, or acknowledgement? Unresolved.
- The **"eight consecutive weeks"** figure appears once, is unsourced, and does not align with Gate 3 landing at months 4–6.

## 5. The governance load is disproportionate — and strategically self-defeating

Four gates, fourteen circulation functions, ExCo sign-off, and roughly six months before anything reaches a customer — in a market where the document itself identifies the winning comparator as an individual on a messaging app who answers personally in eleven minutes at nine in the evening. The irony is unmissable and a reviewer will use it.

**Missing and important: a no-regret fast track running in parallel from week 1.** Actions that require no gate because they cannot be wrong:

- Raise frontline discretionary resolution limits immediately (a bounded pool; measure, don't debate)
- Fix the top three root causes already known to Care Ops without waiting for the taxonomy to be perfected
- Rewrite the twenty highest-volume response templates in-market
- Turn on delivery-exception detection and proactive contact for the single worst failure mode

Absent this track, the programme spends its first quarter producing documents while the satisfaction problem continues to compound. Reframe the gates as *spend-release* gates, not *action-release* gates.

## 6. Substantive omissions, several of them material

- **Vendor/BPO contract structure.** If handling is outsourced on per-contact pricing or committed volumes, "failure-demand elimination funds the programme" may be contractually impossible. Contact removal reduces cost only if the contract permits it. This must be a Gate 0 workstream; currently it is nowhere.
- **Internal chargeback of failure demand.** The single strongest lever implied but never proposed: bill the cost of contacts to the *originating* function (Logistics, Payments, Merchandising) rather than to Care. This changes root-cause behaviour permanently and costs nothing to implement. Its absence is the biggest missed idea in the document.
- **Compensation exposure is the largest number in the plan and the least analysed.** 3–8 bps of GOV exceeds the net programme ask of 1–4 bps. No per-customer cap, no abuse/gaming model, no fraud controls, no stop-loss, no precedent-consistency policy. Finance will stop reading here.
- **Regulatory and legal divergence.** Consumer law on refund timing, return rights, and COD handling varies sharply by market. A published guarantee may create enforceable obligations beyond statutory minimums. Legal is on the circulation list but has no workstream.
- **Labour and works-council implications** of collapsing escalation tiers, in-market hiring, and evening/weekend coverage. Unaddressed.
- **Platform dependency and consent** for messaging-app channels (template approval regimes, per-message costs, data protection, opt-in mechanics). Mentioned as an opportunity, never as an operational constraint.
- **Market intake.** The request specifies "a specific regional market," yet the document never asks which, and adapts to nothing local: COD share, card penetration, address-system quality, dominant super-app, courier fragmentation, language/dialect count, literacy and voice-note preference. It claims locality while remaining generic. Add a one-page market characteristics intake that must be completed before Gate 1 design.

## 7. Measurement is asserted, not built

Rejecting average CSAT and chatbot deflection targets is correct and well argued. But no replacement metric set is offered. It needs to exist on the decision sheet, not in a missing §7.2. Minimum viable set:

- Contacts per 1,000 orders, split value vs failure demand (the headline metric)
- Repeat-contact rate and touches-per-issue distribution (P50/P90)
- Time-to-truth, not time-to-first-response
- First-contact resolution *with authority exercised*
- Root-cause closure rate against the ranked top ten
- Silent-defector rate: 90-day repeat purchase after an unreported failure event vs matched control
- Cost per *resolved* issue (not per contact)
- Segment-level NPS/retention for recoverable defectors only

Likewise, "a held-out design" is stated without a design. In a single regional market, a clean holdout may be infeasible (contamination, small n, seasonality). Specify: geo-split or cohort-randomised, powered against a declared minimum detectable effect, with the stop thresholds written before Gate 3 as promised in §10.2 — which is missing.

## 8. Tone and internal politics

The register is confident to the point of lecturing ("Aggregate scores are the least informative artefact we hold"; "said once and plainly"). More consequentially, the four items in "authority to refuse" include at least one a commercial leader may legitimately need to override — a competitive response if a rival announces a service move mid-pilot. Reframe as *escalation triggers with a named exception path*, or the document will lose credibility on first contact with the Executive Committee. Also: no single accountable owner (DRI) is named, and the "local pod" has no defined composition or mandate.

## 9. Smaller points

- "Five weeks" for transcript mining, blind translation review, silent-defector cohort construction and promise-history archaeology is optimistic — particularly given the document's own contingency that "the record is too thin." Add contingency and a partial-answer path.
- The 55–75% failure-demand benchmark is unsourced. Cite it or label it as a hypothesis with a named owner, per the document's own convention.
- Annex A is referenced but does not exist, so no assumption has an owner — undercutting the central promise of the numbers convention.
- "Version 1. Draft for correction, not for approval" sits awkwardly beside a decision sheet requesting funding today. Pick one.

## 10. What to keep — this is genuinely strong

- The value-demand / failure-demand sort as the organising spine, with every intervention filed under one or the other
- The silent-defector workstream — usually the largest and least-instrumented cohort, and rarely surfaced in plans like this
- The promise-history audit ("customers keep receipts")
- "Authority, not empathy" as the diagnosis of tiering, and the informal messaging-app seller as the benchmark
- Pre-agreed decision rules written before anyone is invested in the answer
- Explicitly declining to charge the programme with retaining price-first, platform-promiscuous buyers
- Refusing deflection/containment as a chatbot objective

## Priority fixes, in order

1. **Write §4A–E.** Concrete, costed, sequenced interventions. Without these there is no answer to the brief.
2. **Rebuild the funding table.** Fix Years 1–2 and steady state; declare the cost-base-to-GOV ratio; state whether gate costs are inside or additive.
3. **Add the parallel no-regret track** starting week 1, and reframe gates as spend-release only.
4. **Add the failure-demand chargeback mechanism** and the **BPO contract audit** to Gate 0.
5. **Cap and control the compensation pool**; give it its own risk section.
6. **Build the metric set and the pilot design** onto the decision sheet.
7. **Fix the segment arithmetic**; add the market-characteristics intake.
8. **Resolve the silence-vs-acknowledgement contradiction** and justify or drop the eight-week rule.
9. **Name a single accountable owner**, define the pod, and add an exception path to the four refusals.
10. **Populate Annex A** so every number has an owner, as promised.
